meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you are born poor it's not your mistake, but if you die poor it's your mistake'?
meta.ogDescription: No speech, book or interview has ever been produced. The line surfaces in a 1997 chain letter with no name on it at all.

answer.label: Not Bill Gates — an unsigned chain letter
answer.authorDates: Credited to Bill Gates (b. 1955), Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist
answer.sourceLine: No speech, interview, book, letter or transcript has ever been produced for this sentence. Quote Investigator ↗ found no substantive evidence linking it to Bill Gates. The earliest strong match it located is a get-rich-quick chain letter posted to Usenet on 21 February 1997 — carrying no attribution at all, and using “fault” where the modern version says “mistake.” Gates’s name is attached only later, in a forwarded email of 2008.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — no source has ever been produced, and the credit to Gates postdates the line by eleven years.

source.excerpt: IT’S NOT YOUR FAULT THAT YOU WERE BORN POOR…AND IF YOU DIE POOR, IT’S YOUR BIGGEST FAULT !!!!
trail: August 1903 — the earliest thematic ancestor QI records: Muriel Strode, in “Wind-Wafted Wild Flowers” in The Open Court, writes “It is no stigma to wear rags; the disgrace is in continuing to wear them.” We confirmed this in the scanned issue (Internet Archive ↗).

December 1909 — the poet Ella Wheeler Wilcox publishes an essay, “To Achieve—Be Positive,” containing the closest match of all: it is not your fault that you were born in poverty, “but it depends upon yourself entirely whether you remain all your life in poverty” (Quote Investigator ↗).
21 February 1997 — the modern shape appears on Usenet inside a chain letter, in capitals, with no name attached (Quote Investigator ↗).

1 June 2008 — a forwarded “Thoughts for the day” email in the Google Group CETAA67 prints the line with “Bill Gates” beneath it and no citation. That is the earliest known credit to him (Quote Investigator ↗).
source.cutTag: A chain letter, not a speech
source.excerptNote: The Usenet posting of 21 February 1997, as transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗. It appears inside a get-rich-quick chain letter and carries no attribution whatsoever. Gates’s name is attached eleven years later, in a forwarded email — which is the whole documented provenance of the credit.

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted: the sentence has no identified author and no authored work behind it — its earliest documented appearance is an anonymous chain letter. The older passages quoted above are a separate matter and are both public domain in the United States, having been published in 1903 and 1909.

author.name: Bill Gates
author.heading: About Bill Gates
author.metaLine: b. 1955 · Microsoft co-founder, software developer and philanthropist
author.bio: Bill Gates co-founded Microsoft in 1975 and has since directed much of his fortune through the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, whose stated mission includes lifting people out of hunger and extreme poverty. That is precisely why the ascription reads oddly: the sentence treats persistent poverty as a personal failing, which is close to the opposite of the premise the philanthropy rests on. Wikiquote ↗ makes the same point and adds a second one — Gates was himself born to an affluent family.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest documented in an anonymous Usenet message posted to the newsgroup news.newusers.questions on 21 February 1997, where the line appears within a chain letter and uses “fault” rather than “mistake,” with no attribution. The earliest known credit to Bill Gates is a forwarded email in the Google Group CETAA67, 1 June 2008, also without citation. Closest documented antecedent: Ella Wheeler Wilcox, “To Achieve—Be Positive,” The Times Dispatch (Richmond, Va.), 21 December 1909, p. 7. Attribution to Gates unverified.

misattribution.heading: A chain letter that acquired a billionaire
misattribution.intro: The line has no author and never did. What it acquired, eleven years after it started circulating, was a name famous enough to make it sound like earned wisdom rather than forwarded email.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ found no substantive evidence that Gates said it. The earliest ascription is a forwarded “Thoughts for the day” email of 1 June 2008, which supplies no citation of any kind.

The strongest early match sits inside a get-rich-quick chain letter posted to Usenet on 21 February 1997, in capitals and with no name on it (Quote Investigator ↗). A line that begins life in a chain letter has no author to recover.

Wilcox’s 1909 essay makes the argument the modern sentence compresses — that being born poor is not your fault, but remaining poor depends on you. QI treats it as the closest documented antecedent, not as the source of this wording (Quote Investigator ↗).

“It is no stigma to wear rags; the disgrace is in continuing to wear them,” from “Wind-Wafted Wild Flowers” in The Open Court, August 1903 — verified in the scan (Internet Archive ↗). The same thought, a century early, and also not this sentence.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator ↗’s conclusion, verbatim: “There is no substantive evidence linking Bill Gates to the modern expression that is often attributed to him.”

context.heading: Why this one sticks to him
lead: The quote works as a Rorschach test. Read one way it is motivational; read another it is a rich man telling the poor that their poverty is a personal failing. Both readings need the same thing to land — a speaker rich enough for the words to carry weight — and Gates is the most available such name in the world.

The documentary record runs the other way. The sentence was already circulating in 1997, unsigned, inside the kind of forwarded chain letter that promises to make you wealthy. It picked up a byline in 2008 the way such messages always do: someone added a famous name at the bottom, and the forwarding did the rest.
context.detailsSummary: The older versions, and why they are better
detailsBody: The thought is genuinely old. Ella Wheeler Wilcox put it carefully in 1909: it is not your fault you were born in the depths of poverty, and not another’s merit that he was born a prince — but what you do from there is yours. She was making an argument, with a concession built into it, and she signed her name (Quote Investigator ↗).

Six years earlier, Muriel Strode had written the same idea as an aphorism: “It is no stigma to wear rags; the disgrace is in continuing to wear them.” It sits in the Miscellaneous pages of The Open Court for August 1903, a few lines below the sentence Strode is actually famous for — “I will not follow where the path may lead, but I will go where there is no path, and I will leave a trail” — which is itself routinely misattributed to Emerson. We read both in the scanned issue (Internet Archive ↗).
context.pull: A line that begins life in a chain letter has no author to recover.
